name: Maryland bridge
lead: A Maryland bridge, also called a resin-bonded or adhesive bridge, replaces a missing tooth with a pontic (false tooth) held by metal or ceramic 'wings' bonded to the etched enamel of the neighbouring teeth, so little or no drilling of those teeth is needed.[1][2] For appearance, it fills a visible gap, most often a single front tooth, with a fixed tooth-coloured replacement without cutting down healthy neighbours for crowns.

The route to a better-looking smile runs through conservation: because the abutment teeth keep their natural enamel and shape, the neighbours stay unaltered while the gap is closed, and the pontic can be shaped and shaded to match the surrounding teeth.[1][12] Dental reviews describe it as a tooth-saving option when the neighbouring teeth are relatively sound and as one of three standard choices for single-tooth replacement alongside the conventional bridge and the implant.[14]

Published reviews report five-year success rates of roughly 84 to 88 percent for resin-bonded bridges overall, and randomized trials and registered studies continue to compare designs and materials.[10][13] Debonding is the usual failure mode and the main thing patients and dentists discuss.[1]

paras: A resin-bonded bridge is an artificial tooth bonded to one or two abutment teeth. If it is built directly in the mouth from composite resin, the connector between pontic and abutment is the weakest part; the alternative is an indirect bridge in which a metal or ceramic framework spans the space and is bonded with composite.[12] The name 'Maryland bridge' is commonly used for the etched cast-metal version; a 1988 clinical review described it under that name.[2]

Wikipedia's bridge article notes that retainer wings bond to etched enamel, that abutments need little or no preparation and are best when intact, and that connectors should be at least 0.7 mm wide and 2 mm high with the pontic lightly touching the opposing tooth in the bite but not in side-to-side movement.[1]

Designs include fixed-fixed (a wing on each side), fixed-movable and cantilever (a single wing).[1] The cantilever is the most tooth-conserving, is suited to single front teeth and is easy to clean, but its small bonding area limits retention and exposes it to torquing forces.[1] Fixed-fixed designs offer large bonding surfaces; fixed-movable designs let the abutments move independently but are not advised for front or long-span cases.[1]

Materials include cast base-metal alloys (the classic Maryland bridge), zirconia, lithium disilicate, In-Ceram alumina and fibre-reinforced composite.[10] Ceramic frameworks are an alternative to metal ones, and zirconia and lithium-disilicate versions are being studied in registered trials.[7][9] Laboratory work has compared retainer shapes such as grooves and pins for resistance to displacement, and reviewers note that deliberate preparation with grooves and rests improves support and longevity.[3][12]

Indications include replacing a single tooth where neighbours are sound and unrestored, gum health is stable, and where a patient is unsuited to or not ready for an implant; a registered trial has examined anterior resin-bonded restorations in adolescents.[1][15]

Ridge-lap pontics, which sit against the gum and mimic a tooth emerging from it, offer the most natural look among pontic styles, while hygienic and bullet pontics are easier to clean but look less natural.[1]

Wikipedia contrasts resin-bonded bridges with conventional bridges: a conventional bridge needs crowns on the abutment teeth, which means more tooth preparation and a higher risk of pulp damage, while conventional fixed-fixed bridges offer maximum strength and are the most accepted design for longer spans.[1] Implants are listed among the alternatives for single-tooth replacement; the page treats unsuitability for implants (for example bone levels, expense or patient preference) as one reason bridgework is chosen.[1][14]

Advantages given for resin-bonded designs include conservation of tooth structure (especially with single-retainer cantilevers), simple laboratory construction for fixed-fixed versions, and easy cleaning for cantilevers.[1]

Dental sources advise good oral hygiene around any bridge because plaque can cause gum inflammation, cleaning under the pontic with interdental aids, regular review appointments, and treating decay or gum disease before and after placement.[1] Because a debonded wing may go unnoticed, regular checks are part of follow-up.[1]

A debonded wing can allow decay to develop beneath it if it goes unnoticed.[1] Contraindications listed include bruxism or other parafunction, mobile teeth, malaligned teeth, long edentulous spans, abutments with little enamel or heavy restorations, nickel or base-metal allergy, and active dental disease.[1]

A literature review of single-retainer anterior bridges examined whether material choice changes survival, and a Dutch review notes there is disagreement over whether two-unit versions outperform three-unit ones.[11][12]

A meta-analysis of human trials and cohort studies reported an estimated five-year success rate of 88.18 percent for metal-framework resin-bonded bridges and 84.41 percent for non-metal frameworks (zirconia 92.07 percent, In-Ceram alumina 94.26 percent, fibre-reinforced composite 84.83 percent). Failure rates did not differ significantly between single, double and multiple retainers, and technical complications were the leading cause of failure.[10]

A long-term randomized trial compared cantilevered with fixed-fixed bridges for missing upper incisors, and a trial of molar replacement compared two-unit cantilevers with three-unit fixed-movable designs.[13][16] A 1988 clinical review covered the etched cast resin-bonded bridge, and clinical-technique papers reported long-term results and guidelines.[2][4][5] Registered randomized trials have studied cantilever bridges for molars, zirconia and lithium-disilicate versions, and no-preparation designs.[6][7][8][9]

card.summary: A winged bridge glued to neighbouring teeth to replace a missing tooth with little drilling; debonding is the usual failure.
card.note: Not suited to grinders, mobile teeth or nickel allergy.

quick.overview:
A Maryland bridge replaces a missing tooth, often a front tooth, using a false tooth with wings glued behind the adjacent teeth.

It preserves more natural tooth than a conventional bridge because little preparation is needed.
quick.mechanism: The wings are bonded to acid-etched enamel on the lingual surface of neighbouring teeth, holding the pontic in the gap.
quick.risks: Debonding is the main concern and can let decay start under a loose wing; contraindications include grinding, mobile teeth and nickel allergy.

chain: Wings bond to enamel on the back of neighbouring teeth
Pontic fills the gap with minimal tooth preparation
Visible gap in the smile is closed while neighbours stay natural
angle.text: A Maryland bridge closes the visible gap left by a missing tooth, most often an upper front tooth, using a fixed false tooth glued behind its neighbours. Because the neighbours need little or no cutting, the smile line is restored while healthy enamel is kept intact.
